What's the purpose of modular arithmetic?

It's a way of calculating in "circles."

The easiest way of thinking about it is with binary, since you can ONLY work with 1's and 0's:

When you add two 0's, you get another 0, which isn't very interesting. When you add a 1 to a 0, you get a 1, which also follows our needs. But, when you add two 1's, you get something that "breaks" our system of using only binary numbers... a 2. So, here, we use modular arithmetic and round that extra integer (past the first 1) back to the beginning, and we get 1 + 1 = 0 so that we get an answer that follows our rules.

It's used a LOT in encryption, since each letter in a lranguage is given a number (A=0, B=1, C=2, etc) and a string of text is changed to a string of numbers (CAT=2, 0, 19). We can now use this numerical string to do a Caesar Cipher, and "shift" all of our letters by 7 integers: 2+7=9, 0+7=7, 19+7=26.

This new string (9, 7, 26) gives us 9=J, 7=H, and 26 gives us nonsense since there are only 26 letters in the English language. But, if we use modular arithmetic, 26 suddenly goes back around and becomes 0, and it gives us an "A" for our ciphertext. So, now, instead of getting a ciphertext that can't be used, we get "cat" turning into "JHA" with the Caesar Cipher.

It's also used a lot in programming. Consider looping through an array, which only has an X number of items. You can't put information in X+1 columns, but you can go back to the beginning and overwrite what's in the first column and just constantly write information in from that point (again), right? In other words, if there are 5 columns for information, you can input 5 pieces of data, then go back to the first position and overwrite everything again, right?

You can do that with a modulus % operator:

int myArray[5];
int x = 0;

while( true ){
 myArray[x] = data;

 x = (x++) % 5;
}

This will continuously increment x from 0 to 5, and beyond. But, since our array can only hold 5 items (as stated by the first line), when x = 5 we will get an error, as there is only five slots: 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4. But the modulus % returns a value of 0 when we use it as 5 % 5, so it will point back at the beginning of the array. This way, we can continue to iterate through x without worrying that it will ever go outside of the realms of our array.

There are literally an unlimited number of ways to use modular arithmetic, but those are the two most common: encryption and programming. The more you learn about it and use it, the more opportunities you'll see where you can use it. Like all math, you're only limited by your imagination and aptitude.

Nearly all of them do. When you "shift" things, you have to consider what you're going to do at the "ends," and using modular arithmetic just makes sense. Regardless of if you're using binary bits (like in the first example) or actual letters (like in my second example), the same concept can be applied.
